routes.description: Establish that consciousness, intentionality, agency, and personal identity cannot be exhausted by physical descriptions, then identify a single nonphysical subject capable of persisting independently of its present body and entering later embodiment.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the mental features and identity conditions require a nonphysical bearer, bodily dependence is compatible with that bearer's continued existence, and a coherent mechanism or argument supports survival beyond bodily death.

motionBridge.description: Show that a conscious person includes one nonphysical subject whose identity can continue after the present organism dies.

centralBridges.description: Establish that phenomenal character or intrinsic intentionality is not captured by an exclusively physical inventory.
Connect irreducible mental properties to a single subject that bears and unifies the person's mental states.
Supply identity conditions under which that subject can remain the same person across bodily discontinuity or renewed embodiment.
Explain why dependence of embodied capacities on the brain does not entail destruction of the subject when the brain ceases functioning.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use reason-responsive agency or freedom to reinforce the distinction between mentality and bottom-up physical causation.
Provide cosmological or probabilistic support for recurrence or another opportunity for postmortem embodiment.

routes.description: Account for consciousness, intentionality, agency, and personal unity as properties or activities of natural organisms at appropriate explanatory scales, while challenging any inference from mental distinctiveness to a separable enduring substance.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic organism-level explanations accommodate the cited mental phenomena, brain dependence undermines an independently functioning bearer, and the proposed identity or cosmological grounds for postmortem survival are not required.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conscious person is a natural organism and that no independently surviving nonphysical subject is needed.

centralBridges.description: Explain mental properties at the organismic scale without reducing them to microphysical vocabulary or adding another substance.
Give physicalist-compatible accounts of phenomenal knowledge, intentional attitudes, and unified consciousness.
Use the systematic dependence of mental capacities on brain states and integrity to oppose separable personal existence.
Challenge the identity conditions and cosmological premises offered to support recurrence or postmortem persistence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve deliberation and reason-responsive action through compatibilist or higher-scale causal explanation.
Relate the onset and loss of conscious capacities to the presence of suitable neural organization.

sections.title: Phenomenal consciousness and physical explanation
sections.rationale: The status of qualia and phenomenal knowledge determines whether first-person experience supplies evidence for facts or properties beyond a natural physical account.

sections.title: Intentionality, mental causation, and agency
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of aboutness, reason-responsive action, and higher-level causation test whether mental activity requires a nonphysical source or fits an organismic framework.

sections.title: From nonphysical properties to subjects and personal identity
sections.rationale: The motion concerns substances rather than merely unusual properties, making the inference to a unified subject and its criteria of persistence an indispensable burden.

sections.title: Cosmology, recurrence, and postmortem survival
sections.rationale: The temporal probability argument, recurrence mechanism, and rival cosmological models bear on whether personal existence can recur after bodily death.

sections.title: Brain dependence, embodiment, and disembodied capacity
sections.rationale: Evidence concerning brain impairment, suitable neural conditions, and the capacities of a disembodied subject bears directly on separability and survival.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Qualia resist physical reduction because their felt first-person character is itself the phenomenon requiring explanation, unlike the mental effects of externally reduced phenomena such as heat.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Huemer, and the uninterrupted answer presents his stated argument from qualia.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents the first-person character of qualia as an explanandum that an exclusively physical inventory must capture.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly develops a central nonphysicality consideration, though the reduction-resistance inference remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The qualia claim and heat contrast are recoverable, with resistance to reduction functioning as an implicit rather than absolute conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The source presents explanatory difficulty rather than a demonstrative refutation, matching the intuitive support actually supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contrast identifies a coherent explanatory demand, but the bridge from first-person character to failed physical reduction is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The bat-style experiential contrast and heat comparison support the explanandum, but rival physical explanations are not seriously compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bridge concerning whether phenomenal character is captured physically.

representationalCharity.rationale: No sufficiently developed rival interpretation is evaluated within this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes first-person experience, the need for similar experience to understand it, and difficulty explaining qualia physically.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Mary's acquisition of experiential knowledge is compatible with identity theory because fully knowing certain physical brain states may require occupying those states.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator turns directly to Oppy, whose extended answer identifies his identity theory and applies it to the Mary case.

components.text: It contacts the demand that physicalism explain privileged first-person access to qualitative experience.

response.rationale: The reply offers a physicalist-compatible explanation: complete acquaintance with some brain states may require occupying them, so experiential novelty need not imply nonphysical facts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central first-person-access challenge with a clear identity-theoretic alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The restricted claim about fully knowing certain brain states is clear and explicitly modal rather than universal.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposal is advanced as a live compatibility account, and its limited evidential force is appropriately signaled.

charity.alternative: Experiential knowledge reveals a nonphysical qualitative fact absent from physical knowledge.
charity.decisiveQualification: The physicalist can distinguish knowing descriptions of a state from fully knowing it by occupying it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The state-acquaintance distinction coherently blocks the immediate inference to nonphysical facts, with one implicit account of full knowledge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The brain-state proposal is relevant and specific, but the claim that occupation is required is not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports a central physicalist-compatible account of phenomenal knowledge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply takes the experiential novelty seriously and answers it without reducing it merely to a verbal confusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies perceptual states with brain states and asks whether their experiential dimension can be fully known only by being in them.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Reality contains scale-specific properties that cannot be defined from lower-scale properties, without making the lower scale metaphysically privileged or abandoning naturalism.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy announces that he will explain his own view and delivers a sustained first-person account of properties across physical scales.

components.text: It replaces microphysical definability with natural explanation at the scale where qualitative properties occur.

response.rationale: The reply justifies a multiscale naturalist demand: failure of lower-scale definition need not imply nonphysicality because natural properties may be autonomous at higher scales.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves the explanatory issue and directly denies that irreducibility to lower-scale vocabulary establishes nonnatural properties.

precisionFindings.rationale: Scale, lower-scale definability, autonomy, and naturalism remain distinguishable and the claim is explicitly generalized across scales.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The multiscale account is offered as a defensible naturalist framework rather than as a completed derivation of consciousness.

charity.alternative: If qualitative properties cannot be reduced to microphysical properties, they are nonphysical.
charity.decisiveQualification: Non-definability from a lower scale can indicate scale autonomy without placing the property outside nature.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between scale autonomy and metaphysical privilege is clear, though its application to qualia retains an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Chemical and other scale examples support the framework, but its success for phenomenal properties is not specifically demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central multiscale-naturalism bridge at a high position within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the irreducibility intuition while disputing the inference from irreducibility to metaphysical nonphysicality.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asserts that chemical and other scale-specific properties may be autonomous from lower-scale definition without leaving naturalism.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Mary gains propositional knowledge of a determinate qualitative property, not merely an ability, because seeing red rules out alternative ways that the experience could have felt.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly solicits Huemer's response, and Huemer directly contrasts his fact-based interpretation with Oppy's skills account.

components.text: It directly disputes that Mary's novelty is exhausted by ability or state acquaintance.
It supplies a determinate qualitative fact but does not directly refute the scale-specific naturalist classification of that fact.

response.rationale: The reply argues that seeing red eliminates qualitative possibilities and therefore supplies propositional knowledge, directly contacting the acquaintance account but not the separate multiscale-naturalist ontology.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive Mary component clearly while leaving the independent scale-specific naturalist response unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fact claimed, its qualitative alternatives, and the evidential elimination relation are stated with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ruling out qualitative possibilities supports new propositional discrimination, but does not by itself establish that the fact is nonphysical.

charity.alternative: Mary acquires only an ability or acquaintance by entering the relevant physical state.
charity.decisiveQualification: Her experience also discriminates among ways the qualitative character could have been.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The possibility-elimination argument coherently supports new propositional knowledge, though the route to nonphysicality remains unstated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The determinate red-experience example supports the epistemic claim, but competing modes-of-presentation accounts are not resolved.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central phenomenal-functional account through the Mary case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly identifies what the acquaintance view captures and adds a specific propositional-content challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Mary learns that seeing red is like this because her first experience rules out alternative qualitative characters.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Qualia and intentionality support property dualism, while the problem of personal identity provides the further route from nonphysical properties to substance dualism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the intentionality question to Huemer, and the uninterrupted answer develops his stated dualist argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move identifies personal identity as the required bridge from allegedly nonphysical mental properties to a substance bearing them.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It correctly identifies the indispensable bridge but supplies little of the personal-identity argument needed to complete it.

precisionFindings.rationale: Property dualism, substance dualism, and the proposed personal-identity bridge are distinguishable and cautiously stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move acknowledges that a further argument is required, though saying the remaining step is not far understates its burden.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but the crucial inference from irreducible properties to one substance is asserted rather than supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on prior qualia and intentionality claims and provides no developed identity evidence within this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the indispensable central bridge from mental properties to a unified subject.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span announces a route rather than engaging a developed competing interpretation of that route.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly separates property dualism from substance dualism and says personal identity is needed to connect them.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Tree rings have no intrinsic aboutness; they function as evidence only because observers interpret them through mental states that represent the tree's age.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange directly follows a challenge posed to Huemer, and his answer distinguishes intrinsic from derivative intentionality.

components.text: It challenges a naturalized example of aboutness by distinguishing intrinsic representation from observer-derived evidence.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that tree rings possess only derivative intentionality because mental interpreters, rather than the rings themselves, represent the tree's age.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the naturalized-aboutness example and identifies the precise intrinsic-versus-derivative distinction at issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: Intrinsic and derivative intentionality are used consistently, and the claim is restricted to the tree-ring example.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interpretive account is presented with modest language and is adequately fitted to the illustrative case.

charity.alternative: Tree rings are about a tree's age because they reliably carry information about it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reliability as evidence may depend on an interpreting mental state and therefore establish only derivative aboutness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is coherently applied, though the general conclusion that only mentality has intrinsic aboutness remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The tree-ring analysis is a clear example, but one example does not exclude all naturalistic accounts of intrinsic content.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports mental nonphysicality, though intentionality is only one part of that central bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the informational relation and fairly explains why it may not amount to intrinsic intentionality.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says rings are merely evidence and that the observer's mental state, not the rings, represents the tree's age.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Functionalist accounts can explain intentional attitudes within identity theory, making intentionality less troublesome for physicalism than consciousness or qualia.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Oppy, whose answer contrasts physicalist treatments of intentionality with the harder qualia problem.

components.text: It answers the aboutness challenge by invoking functionalist accounts of beliefs, desires, and intentional attitudes.

response.rationale: The reply directly supplies a physicalist-compatible family of accounts for intentional attitudes, while conceding that consciousness and qualia present a harder problem.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the intentionality demand clearly, although it cites the functionalist option more than it develops its mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully restricted to intentional attitudes and explicitly distinguishes them from consciousness and qualia.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Functionalism is presented as a reasonable account rather than a conclusive solution, appropriately matching the abbreviated warrant.

charity.alternative: Intrinsic aboutness cannot be derived from nonintentional physical relations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Functional roles may constitute belief and desire content even if qualia remain independently difficult.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Functionalism is a coherent possible answer, but the bridge from functional role to genuinely intrinsic content is not developed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a recognized explanatory structure but gives no representative functional analysis or comparison with the derivative-content objection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central physicalist-compatible account of intentional attitudes.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response targets the strongest intentionality concern while expressly avoiding an overbroad claim about phenomenal consciousness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says identity theorists can also be functionalists and obtain a reasonable account of beliefs, desires, and aboutness.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Macroscopic indeterminacy does not yield libertarian freedom, while action from normally acquired beliefs and desires without defeating interference supplies sufficient compatibilist freedom.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Oppy for his response, and the sustained answer states both his indeterminist cosmology and compatibilist account of agency.

components.text: It contests the need for an extra substance by offering organism-level compatibilist conditions for free action.

response.rationale: The reply rejects libertarian freedom as unnecessary and substitutes action from normally acquired beliefs and desires without defeating interference as sufficient freedom.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the agency-based pressure on physicalism, although it does not directly address the separate property-to-substance identity bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: Libertarian and compatibilist freedom are kept distinct, and the proposed sufficient conditions are reasonably clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents an inclined compatibilist position and does not claim that the short account settles every freedom dispute.

charity.alternative: Genuine freedom requires the ability to do otherwise in a libertarian sense.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reason-guided action without abnormal interference may satisfy the practical freedom condition even under physical causation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibilist criterion is internally coherent, though its sufficiency rather than merely stipulative adequacy is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The beliefs-and-desires account is specific but receives little support against manipulation or sourcehood objections.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary natural-agency bridge within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply states the libertarian demand before offering a substantive compatibilist replacement rather than caricaturing it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies strong libertarian freedom and defines free action through normally acquired beliefs and desires without interfering defeat.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Emergent or downward-causal organization does not establish substance dualism because higher-scale events remain events occurring in the brain, without an additional mental substance.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy answers the suggestion that dualists would claim victory and explicitly distinguishes the emergent story from the existence of mental substances.

components.text: It identifies that higher-scale or downward causation does not entail an additional substance bearing mental events.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the inference failure: all cited higher-scale activity may remain brain activity, so emergence alone supplies no premise establishing another mental substance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive property-to-substance inference and states the consequence for substance dualism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between higher-scale brain events and an additional mental substance is concise and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that the described emergence story does not itself establish another substance follows from the absent premise.

charity.alternative: Downward-causal or emergent mental organization indicates a distinct mental substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinct causal organization can consist entirely in events occurring in the brain without a second bearer.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference diagnosis is clear and valid, with only the broader positive organismic ontology left outside this short span.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is conceptual and directly tied to the described story, though no detailed emergent model is provided.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central bridge from nonphysical properties or causation to a separate subject.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants higher-scale organization and targets only the unsupported ontological inference to an extra substance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says no mental substance appears in the proposed story because human-scale events remain events happening in the brain.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: If time is infinite in both directions and each person lives only once, the probability of being alive now is zero; therefore reincarnation occurs or the infinite-past assumption is false.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Huemer to present his argument, and the ensuing uninterrupted answer uses his stated assumptions and conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move uses an infinite-past sampling argument to support recurrence, while allowing rejection of the infinite-past premise as the alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a clear dilemma relevant to cosmological support, but its probability measure and link to personal recurrence remain underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The assumptions and dilemma are explicit, but the reference class and probability of being alive at a specific time are not fully fixed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The zero-probability conclusion depends on an unstated sampling measure, so the dilemma is stronger than the supplied warrant supports.

charity.alternative: A person can live once in an infinite past and future without being randomly sampled from all times.
charity.decisiveQualification: The zero-probability inference requires a justified temporal self-location measure rather than infinity alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dilemma is intelligible, but the unsupported uniform-sampling premise creates a substantial gap in the zero-probability inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The fact of present existence is invoked, but neither the temporal measure nor recurrence mechanism is independently supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary cosmological bridge and sits near the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument states its temporal alternatives but omits the strongest measure-theoretic qualification to its probability premise.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt assumes infinite past and future time, single lives, and infers that the chance of being alive specifically now would be zero.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Contemporary cosmology makes a finite past and infinite future more plausible than an infinite past, while expansion and entropy considerations also undermine cosmic recurrence.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly contrasts Huemer's temporal view with the view favored by physics and supplies cosmological and entropy-based considerations.

components.text: It rejects the dilemma's infinite-past premise by appealing to a finite-past, infinite-future cosmology.

response.rationale: The reply directly selects and supports the dilemma's permitted alternative, adding expansion and entropy considerations against recurrent cosmic conditions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the vulnerable cosmological premise and also addresses the recurrence assumption underlying the proposed support.

precisionFindings.rationale: Finite past, infinite future, recurrence, expansion, and entropy are clearly separated and comparatively qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The view is presented as more plausible under contemporary physics, not as metaphysically certain.

charity.alternative: Time is infinite in both directions, activating the reincarnation dilemma.
charity.decisiveQualification: A finite-past cosmology avoids the dilemma, and recurrence requires further physical conditions not supplied by infinity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Rejecting the infinite-past premise coherently blocks the dilemma, with the empirical cosmology warrant appropriately separated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Contemporary cosmology, expansion, and entropy are specific supports, though documentation and rival-model comparison remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary cosmological-support bridge at the top of its tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses both temporal extent and recurrence rather than treating the argument as depending on only one premise.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts the infinite-past view with a physics-favored finite past and separately raises expansion, entropy, and recurrence concerns.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Standard projections of an eternally expanding universe imply eventual proton and black-hole decay followed only by sparse radiation, so stars, people, and recurrent conditions never return.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers Huemer's finite-cycling premise and describes the long-term cosmological future presented as the serious physical projection.

components.text: It challenges the recurrence route by describing an expanding future in which complex conditions never return.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies the physical recurrence premise through a concrete heat-death projection involving proton decay, black-hole decay, and sparse radiation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the recurrence mechanism, although it does not independently address the argument's self-location probability premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The projection is clearly restricted to standard eternally expanding cosmology and distinguishes its successive future stages.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The standard projection supports a strong expectation, though categorical language about nonreturn exceeds the excerpt's compressed model comparison.

charity.alternative: Infinite future duration makes repeated stars, organisms, or personal conditions inevitable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Under continuing expansion and heat death, unlimited duration need not regenerate low-entropy complex structures.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The heat-death sequence coherently undermines recurrence conditional on the projected cosmology, with that condition clearly identifiable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific decay stages provide representative support, but alternative cosmological models and fluctuation possibilities are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary cosmological-support bridge with a concrete nonrecurrence model.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply directly addresses the intuitive infinity-to-recurrence inference with a physically specified countermodel.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes black-hole decay, continuing expansion, sparse radiation, and the nonreturn of protons, stars, and people.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Blind bottom-up physical causes cannot ground free will because they do not respond to reasons, whereas causation by a higher-level mental subject can make conduct reason-responsive.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the question to Huemer, and the ensuing first-person answer restates and develops Huemer's earlier free-will argument.

components.text: It disputes that action caused by physical beliefs and desires is sufficiently reason-responsive for genuine freedom.
It proposes higher-level mental causation but does not establish that its higher-level cause is an additional substance.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the compatibilist agency criterion by contrasting blind bottom-up causes with reason-responsive mental causation, but it leaves the no-extra-substance diagnosis unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the agency component while failing to answer the distinct demand for an inference to another substance.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is recoverable, but 'respond to reasons' shifts between causes possessing reasons and behavior tracking reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Claiming that only a higher-level mental cause permits freedom exceeds the argument because physical systems may implement reason sensitivity.

charity.alternative: Physical belief-desire processes can implement sensitivity to reasons without causes themselves having reasons.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply treats bottom-up causes as blind but does not exclude higher-scale physical reason responsiveness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument equivocates between a cause having reasons and a system responding to reasons, leaving the exclusivity inference unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The blind-cause characterization is asserted and does not compare compatibilist models of higher-scale physical control.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary agency bridge, though it does not complete a substance inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The physicalist alternative is materially weakened by moving from nonconscious microcauses to the absence of organism-level reason tracking.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls physical causes blind and nonresponsive to reasons, then claims freedom requires causation by the higher-level mental thing.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: A resemblance-based account of personal identity does not readily support reincarnation as an animal because an animal would not be a qualitative duplicate of the person.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly challenges Huemer's reincarnation proposal by invoking the resemblance and duplication conditions from Huemer's own personal-identity argument.

components.text: It challenges the personal-identity consequence by showing that recurrence alone does not identify a later animal as the same person.
The cross-species resemblance objection does not contact the separate reason-responsive causation argument.

response.rationale: The reply directly raises a missing identity condition for animal reincarnation: a dog or other animal would not be the qualitative duplicate required by the resemblance account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive personal-identity limitation of the recurrence proposal, while leaving the agency move outside its scope.

precisionFindings.rationale: Resemblance, qualitative duplication, and cross-species reincarnation are clearly distinguished and the objection is cautiously framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is limited to a prima facie gap in the resemblance account and matches the illustrative support.

charity.alternative: A future animal could be the same person through sufficient resemblance or qualitative duplication.
charity.decisiveQualification: Large cross-species differences make the required duplicate relation unclear without an independent soul-identity criterion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection coherently exposes a mismatch between duplication-based identity and cross-species embodiment, subject to further identity criteria.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dog comparison is apt, but the exact resemblance threshold and full personal-identity theory are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central personal-persistence bridge through a concrete identity-condition gap.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply uses the proponent's resemblance condition and identifies a specific case where its application becomes difficult.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says qualitative duplication matters to the identity account and observes that a dog is not sufficiently similar to the person.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Reincarnation need not depend on eternal recurrence or qualitative duplication, because unknown conditions might instead cause an enduring soul to enter another living organism.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer recounts in the first person how multiverse duplication inspired his argument and then distinguishes that route from an alternative involving a persisting soul.

components.text: It replaces duplicate-based recurrence with persistence of one soul through embodiment in another organism.
It explains why cosmic recurrence is unnecessary but supplies no positive reembodiment mechanism beyond unknown conditions.

response.rationale: The reply justifies separating soul reembodiment from qualitative duplication and eternal recurrence, preserving the survival question through identity of an enduring soul.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers the duplicate and recurrence objections at the level of possibility, but the replacement mechanism is explicitly unknown.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative is clearly modal and distinguishes an enduring soul route from recurrence and duplicate-based routes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Unknown embodiment conditions are offered only as a possibility, which matches the very limited warrant.

charity.alternative: Without recurrence or a qualitative duplicate, no later organism satisfies the proposed identity relation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Identity could instead be secured by numerical persistence of one soul, if such a soul and embodiment conditions exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative is logically possible, but it presupposes the enduring soul whose identity and attachment mechanism require support.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposed unknown conditions are speculative and provide no evidence that reembodiment actually occurs or is physically available.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central survival-underdetermination bridge by supplying an alternative identity route, albeit weakly warranted.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly isolates the duplication objection and provides a coherent conditional alternative, while acknowledging its unknown conditions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says eternal recurrence is not essential and suggests that unknown conditions might cause an existing soul to enter a living thing.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: A soul is the single subject bearing all of a person's rational thoughts, sensations, and emotions, rather than an additional rational entity distinct from the ordinary subject of experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Huemer by name, and Huemer answers by explicitly defining what he means by a soul and applying that definition to rational thought, sensation, and emotion.

components.text: It identifies the soul with the ordinary unified subject rather than positing a second rational subject.
Defining one current subject does not answer the cross-species persistence or resemblance condition.

response.rationale: The reply clarifies what the alleged substance is by unifying rational thought, sensation, and emotion in one subject, but it does not establish that this subject is nonphysical or persists.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the bearer question but leaves the decisive extra-substance inference and persistence challenge substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The soul is consistently defined as the single subject of the person's diverse mental states.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Unity of ordinary experience supports one subject, but confidently labeling that subject a soul does not establish its nonphysical nature.

charity.alternative: One organism or brain can be the unified subject without an additional soul.
charity.decisiveQualification: Phenomenal unity identifies a bearer but does not by itself determine whether that bearer is physical or nonphysical.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The unity claim is coherent, but the inference from one subject of experience to one nonphysical substance remains materially missing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Shared ownership of thoughts, sensations, and emotions supports unity, not the further ontological classification asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central subject-from-properties bridge, though it does not complete that bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The clarification avoids a two-subject caricature, yet omits the strongest organismic interpretation of the same unity evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines the soul as the same single subject that has rational thoughts, sensations, emotions, and other mental states.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Souls have always existed rather than emerging through evolution, but a soul can inhabit an organism only when suitable physical conditions, such as a brain capable of supporting intelligence, arise.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Huemer to clarify his answer, and Huemer states both the eternal existence of souls and the bodily conditions required for embodied life.

components.text: It supplies a soul-based embodiment condition that does not require qualitative duplication across organisms.
It asserts preexisting souls but does not answer the demand for evidence of an additional nonphysical bearer.
It makes embodiment depend on suitable brains but does not answer whether future suitable organisms will exist.

response.rationale: The reply gives a conditional account of when an eternal soul may inhabit an organism, contacting embodiment compatibility but not evidencing eternal souls or future opportunities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary embodiment component while leaving the decisive existence and future-survival premises unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: Eternal existence, inhabitation, suitable physical conditions, and brain-supported intelligence are distinguishable and openly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The embodiment conditions are appropriately tentative, but the claim that souls have always existed lacks corresponding support.

charity.alternative: Subjects arise only when suitable neural organization develops.
charity.decisiveQualification: The proposed soul may preexist while lacking embodiment, but no independent criterion distinguishes this from later subject emergence.
